title: Some things cannot be booked once you're aboard.
subtitle: Specialty dining and the good excursions close before you've unpacked — often before you sail.

text: The best port day of your voyage is usually reserved weeks earlier.
sub: Booking windows open by fare, suite category or loyalty tier, and they differ by line. Ask when yours opens rather than finding out when it closes.

items.head: The one restaurant worth it
items.body: There is usually one, and it fills first. The rest can wait until you are onboard.

items.head: The tour with a hard capacity
items.body: Small-group tours, private guides and anything on the water sell out long before the day.

items.head: The tight-turnaround port
items.body: On a short call, the ship's own excursion is the version that guarantees the ship waits.

title: The cost of leaving it late

left.label: Left late
items: The port day you settle for

right.label: Booked early
items: The port day you came for

text: On the ship's own excursion, a late return is the line's problem.
sub: It waits, or it gets you to the next port at its own cost. On an independent tour it is not required to wait, and the recovery is yours to fund.

quote: Book the reservations you would regret losing. Leave the rest loose — that is what sea days are for.

title: Save this before your booking window opens
body: Send me your sailing and I'll mark the two port days with no margin in them, and the one restaurant worth a note in the diary.
